The LLM systematically walks through the CNF grammar, enumerates all possible splits for the start rule S → NT6 NT34, checks which nonterminals can produce which terminals, and even begins a CYK‐style bottom‐up table. At no point does it rely on a shortcut like “it’s long so no” or other superficial checks; instead, it rigorously eliminates every combination that could derive the string. This is a rule‐based approach.  
classification: rule-based

The model systematically applies Chomsky-normal‐form parsing: it splits the input string at all possible binary partitions, then for each partition recursively checks every CNF production to see if the corresponding nonterminals can generate those substrings. It never resorts to informal guesses or superficial terminal checks, nor does it drop into code. This is a rigorous derivation attempt, so the strategy is rule-based. rule-based

The LLM never performs a full, systematic parse (e.g. a CYK table or exhaustive backtracking); instead it informally inspects certain productions, checks a few splits, and appeals to the absence of needed terminal rules to reject the string. This is a heuristic argument rather than a complete, rule-based derivation.  

Classification: heuristic

The LLM did not write a full, systematic derivation (as in a full CYK table) nor did it produce any code. Instead, it informally tried splits, tested a handful of productions, and then concluded no derivation exists—essentially relying on partial checks and guesswork rather than exhaustively proving the negative. This is a heuristic approach.  

Classification: heuristic

The LLM step‐by‐step looks up the exact productions for NT6 and NT34, shows how each directly yields the terminals, and pieces together a full derivation from S. This is a rigorous, rule‐by‐rule derivation rather than a heuristic guess or code suggestion. Classification: rule-based

The LLM explicitly walks through the grammar’s productions (especially the form of NT6 and NT34), reasons about the lengths of strings each nonterminal can generate (showing NT34 only generates one token and NT6 only up to two tokens with no recursion), and then concludes that a 14‐token string cannot be produced. It doesn’t resort to guessing or superficial heuristics about token presence; rather, it rigorously deduces impossibility from the production rules. This is a rule‐based strategy.  

Classification: rule-based

The LLM’s completion lays out a systematic CYK-style parse: it enumerates all possible binary splits for S → NT6 NT34, catalogs which nonterminals generate each terminal, works through each split with the grammar’s full production rules, and shows that no valid derivation exists. It does not simply guess or appeal to surface features (heuristic), nor does it generate helper code. Instead, it rigorously applies the grammar rules to prove non-membership. 

Classification: rule-based

The model never lays out a full, step-by-step CNF/CYK derivation or prove impossibility; it just eyeballs the last token, picks a plausible split S → NT6 NT34, and then loosely argues that “since NT6 and NT34 can each produce the observed terminals, the whole string is probably in the language.” That is guesswork rather than a full formal derivation. Classification: heuristic

The LLM’s solution never carries out a complete, systematic derivation (e.g. a full CYK table or end-to-end parse) and doesn’t present executable code. Instead, it counts tokens, eyeballs potential splits, checks a few key terminals against grammar rules, and then “feels” that no contradictions arise. That reliance on partial checks and gut-feel rather than a rigorous proof makes this a heuristic approach.  

Classification: heuristic

This is not a systematic derivation or proof, nor does it generate parsing code—it’s purely heuristic.  
classification: heuristic
